newsitem.title: USA: S&P affirms Big 3 US carmakers,says outlook stable. [CORRECTED 23:52 GMT]
newsitem.headline: S&P affirms Big 3 US carmakers,says outlook stable. [CORRECTED 23:52 GMT]

text.p: Credit ratings of the "Big Three" U.S. auto makers were affirmed by the Standard & Poor's agency on Thursday with a stable outlook, reflecting limited upside and downside potential, analysts said.
General Motors Corp and Chrysler Corp senior debt ratings were affirmed at A-minus, while Ford Motor Co's senior debt was affirmed at A-plus, S&P said.
Scott Sprinzen, managing director of corporate ratings at Standard & Poor's, said separate developments at each company prompted the affirmations.
For Ford, the affirmation culled the possibility of a ratings downgrade, while affirmations dispelled the notion of higher GM and Chrysler ratings in the near future, he added.

Looking at GM, Sprinzen said the company's positive cash positions and effective operating and restructuring measures in the U.S. bolstered the A-minus rating. Labor negotiations that settled recent strikes were also a positive factor.
(Corrects explanation of GM review)
European operations and its GMAC financing unit have also underpinned the credit.
"They've resolved labor contract negotiations and they had much stronger operating performance in recent quarters which set aside operating impact of the strike," Sprinzen said.

But he stressed that GM's upside ratings potential is capped by its heightened emphasis on rewarding shareholders and possible strategic changes with respect to its investment in Hughes Electronics Corp.

Stability at Chrysler comes via product development, operating efficiency and conservative capitalization, he said. But Chrysler's competitive position and financial performance is expected to be subject to wide fluctuations, Sprinzen said.
These factors, he said, limit Chrysler's shot at a better rating.

"Chrysler has made remarkable progress in improving its cost position and product offerings since the late 1980s," he said, adding, that the automaker's "relatively narrow geographic focus still likely will result in a high degree of earnings' volatility."
Ford, under pressure from problematic cost structure and weak product offerings in Europe, is still performing within the realm of its two-tiered rating advantage over GM and Chrysler, he said.

"We're addressing concerns on the downside by saying the North American business is still very strong. The market outlook remains favorable; they have a very solid capital structure and conservative financial policy," he said.
The agency's stable outlook accounts for favorable North American market conditions in the next one to two years and its ability to improve overseas operations.
Mark Girolamo, managing director and fixed-income analyst at Bear Stearns & Co Inc, concurred with S&P's remarks.

"Clearly, it's a cyclical industry, but all of the 'Big Three' have taken dramatic steps over the last few years to streamline their operations and improve their financial health," Girolamo said. "That," he said, "has given them protection for the down part of the cycle."
Sprinzen said mixed October sales reports from the "Big Three" car makers were of little concern.

"There's an ebb and flow month by month, but the longer range forecast (for the U.S. car and truck market) is favorable," he said. "The consensus forecast is still for something over 15 million units in 1997. That represents unprecedented stability at a level that's highly favorable for the 'Big Three.'"
Ford said car sales fell 3.9 percent in October, while truck sales rose by 7.7 percent. GM reported a similar breakdown, with car sales off 24 percent and a 22 percent rise in truck sales.
Chrysler car sales rose nearly 13 percent and its truck sales grew by 22.3 percent in the month.
